content: Poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac are plants that frequently cause allergic skin reactions. These reactions typically manifest as an intensely itchy, red rash accompanied by bumps or blisters. Poison ivy is one of the most common causes of skin rashes in both children and adults who spend time outdoors. This plant is found throughout the United States, except in the Southwest, Alaska, and Hawaii. It is characterized by three shiny green leaves and a red stem and often grows as a vine, particularly along riverbanks. Poison oak is primarily located on the West Coast, grows as a shrub, and has three leaves similar to poison ivy. Poison sumac, on the other hand, is abundant along the Mississippi River and grows as a woody shrub with stems containing 7 to 13 leaves arranged in pairs. Symptoms of Poison Ivy Exposure The symptoms of poison ivy exposure include: Severe itching. A red, streaky, or patchy rash at the site of contact with the plant. Red bumps that may develop into large, oozing blisters. The severity of the reaction can vary, ranging from mild to severe. In rare cases, hospitalization may be required. The most intense symptoms typically occur between days 4 and 7 after exposure, and the rash may persist for 1 to 3 weeks. Causes of Poison Ivy Rash The rash is caused by direct skin contact with the oils (resin) of these plants. Inhalation of smoke from burning these plants can also trigger the same reaction. The plant oils penetrate the skin quickly, but the rash is not contagious and does not spread through the fluid from blisters. Once the oils are thoroughly washed off the skin, the rash cannot be transmitted to others. However, the plant oils can remain on contaminated clothing, pets, tools, shoes, and other surfaces for extended periods. If these items are not properly cleaned, they can cause future rashes upon contact. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Call 911 or visit an emergency room if: Someone experiences a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling or difficulty breathing, or has a history of severe reactions. Someone has been exposed to smoke from burning poison ivy, oak, or sumac. Contact a healthcare provider if: The itching is severe and uncontrollable. The rash affects the face, lips, eyes, or genitals. The rash shows signs of infection, such as pus, yellow fluid leaking from blisters, a foul odor, or increased tenderness. Treatment Options Wash the skin thoroughly with soap and warm water as soon as possible, ideally within 30 minutes of exposure, to remove the plant oils. Scrub under the fingernails with a brush to prevent the spread of oils to other parts of the body. Wash contaminated clothing and shoes with soap and hot water, as the plant oils can linger on these items. Bathe pets immediately to remove oils from their fur. Avoid activities that increase body heat and sweating, as these can worsen itching. Instead, stay cool and apply cool compresses to the skin. Use calamine lotion or hydrocortisone cream to reduce itching and blistering. Take lukewarm baths with oatmeal bath products, available at drugstores, to soothe itchy skin. Aluminum acetate (Domeboro solution) soaks can help dry the rash and reduce itching. If creams, lotions, or bathing do not alleviate the itching, antihistamines may be helpful. In severe cases, particularly for rashes on the face or genitals, a healthcare provider may prescribe oral or injectable steroids. Clean tools and other objects with a diluted bleach solution or rubbing alcohol to remove any lingering plant oils. What Not to Do Do not touch skin or clothing that still has plant resins on it. Do not burn poison ivy, oak, or sumac to dispose of it. The resins can become airborne in the smoke and cause severe reactions in people downwind. Prevention of Poison Ivy Rash Wear long sleeves, long pants, and socks when walking in areas where these plants may grow. Apply skin products like Ivy Block lotion beforehand to reduce the risk of a rash. Learn to identify poison ivy, oak, and sumac, and teach children to recognize these plants as well. Remove these plants if they grow near your home, but never burn them. Be aware that pets can carry plant resins on their fur. Wash your skin as soon as possible after suspected exposure to these plants.
